<reason>A very close, high-quality debate. PRO built a principled symmetry case (a worker's dollar equals a consumer's dollar; wage-SSNIP is the same tool; ex post remedies can't manufacture a second employer) and landed a sharp closing blow by exposing CON's [B4.1] bright line as the asymmetry restated rather than defended. But CON narrowed the debate more effectively and kept PRO on a burden it only partly met: what happens in the genuine conflict case. PRO's "condition it" was a legitimate answer, yet CON's "conditioning is counting; parity means labor can veto a measured price gain" framing forced PRO to defend the veto, which PRO never squarely did. CON's [B4.4] turn—that a one-hospital-town merger is already caught on the price side, so surviving scarcity is pre-existing—undercut PRO's flagship example, and PRO dropped it rather than pivoting to cases like meatpacking or warehousing where the product market is national but the labor market is local. CON also directly answered the welfare-equivalence point ("harder to locate, better guarded," not worth less). Both sides had minor clipping. Razor-thin edge to CON for making the decisive question clearer and leaving PRO's strongest example wounded.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A2 in [B4.4]: answering PRO's "quit to whom?" pressure question by noting that a merger creating a single buyer of nurses in a small town also creates a single seller of hospital care, so price-side review already catches it and any remaining scarcity predates the merger. PRO's closing acknowledged the point only glancingly and never rehabilitated the example with cases where labor and product markets diverge.</best_rebuttal>
